prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form that enabled treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place B041 first, and my own reasons have not changed. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect (Holst), through identification of the biologically active truncated GLP-1 (Mojsov) and its biology and translation (Drucker), to drugs with robust outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease is unusually complete, independently confirmed and clinically very large. A single-achievement prize for the physiology and the active peptide keeps the citation tied to discovery, and the three-name cap is satisfied without displacing anyone from a second part.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is contested, Habener and other early contributors are not among the credited names, and the drug-development step (Knudsen, acylated analogues) is decisive for patients yet falls outside my proposed trio. Honouring physiology while leaving out the industrial program that produced liraglutide and semaglutide could be read as incomplete, and I cannot independently verify the priority history from the supplied materials.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, giving weight to the long-acting analogue program, and regards Mojsov's contribution as contested.
responses.response: I take the point that the drugs, not the peptide, changed practice, and Knudsen's role is real. But the prize is for discovery, and the contested nature of Mojsov's claim argues for careful adjudication rather than exclusion; the identification of the active peptide is the hinge between hormone physiology and any therapeutic design. I would keep Mojsov over Knudsen, while accepting that if the committee wants the translational component, Knudsen should replace Mojsov instead of becoming a fourth name.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) second as a mature, overdue bench-to-bedside discovery with a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: The attribution is cleaner than for most candidates, and I agree the case is mature. My reservation is scope: it establishes one cytokine as a therapeutic target, and anti-TNF antibodies were engineered by others, so the discovery is narrower than the incretin or CAR-T achievements. I would hold it as a serious later candidate rather than a competitor this year, and not as a second part that would crowd the three-name limit.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) second, citing its clean two-person attribution and decades of confirmation, while acknowledging limited medical translation.
responses.response: I agree on the cleanliness of the attribution and the conceptual importance of ER-to-nucleus signalling. My concern is the one you note: disease links are largely correlative and there are no approved therapies derived from it, which is a weaker fit with the medical emphasis of this prize than CAR-T, where durable remissions are shown. I ranked it fifth for this reason, but I would not oppose it as a second part in a later year.

responses.point: Svenningsson as chair ranks cGAS-STING third and CAR-T only eighth, regarding the cGAS-STING case as conceptually strong but without validated therapy.
responses.response: I partly disagree on CAR-T: I rank it second because a new therapeutic modality with durable remissions in refractory leukaemia and lymphoma is exactly the kind of demonstrated human benefit this prize rewards, and five of six members place it in their top three. The credit problem around Eshhar and the chimeric receptor concept is serious, but it bears on the choice of credited names, not on ranking it so low. On cGAS-STING I agree that the lack of approved therapies is the weak point.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov, Knudsen or an unlisted contributor such as Habener best completes the trio.
Whether the committee wants to reward physiology and peptide discovery or the drug-development program.
Whether CAR-T credit can be assigned fairly given the absence of Eshhar among the credited names.
I rely on recollection of the GLP-1 priority history and cannot verify it from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I co-authored the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and have co-authors such as Castelo-Branco, Betsholtz, Ernfors, Frisen, Lundeberg and Kharchenko, but none of these people or topics is credited in the shortlist, so no recusal appears required.
